passage:
Dear Diary,
The new van uncle is so nice to me. He lets me sit in front. Today he gave me a sparkly pencil box, only me, not my brother Anand or the others. He said I'm his favourite and it's our special secret.
I liked feeling special. But my tummy felt funny about the secret part. At school Ma'am said no grown-up should ask us to keep secrets from our parents.
So tonight I told Mummy. I thought she'd be angry about the pencil box. She wasn't. She hugged me and said I did exactly right and it's never my fault. Then she called Papa and the school office straight away. From tomorrow Papa is dropping me and Anand to school.
Reena

qa.q: What did the van uncle give Reena?
qa.a: He gave Reena a sparkly pencil box.

qa.q: How did Reena feel about the secret part?
qa.a: Reena liked feeling special but felt uneasy about the secret, with a funny feeling in the tummy that something was not right.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that made telling safe for Reena?
qa.a: Mummy hugged Reena, said it was never Reena's fault, and called Papa and the school office straight away.

qa.q: How might Anand feel when Papa starts dropping them to school?
qa.a: Anand may be curious or a bit surprised by the change, but the new plan keeps both children safe.

grounding: A child enjoys gifts and a special secret from an adult, feels uneasy, tells a parent, and is thanked and protected that same evening.

passage:
After school each day, Thomas stopped at the shop by the paddy fields. The shopkeeper always had something: a free orange lolly, a go on the old video game in the back room. "You're smarter than the other boys," he would say. "Our little secret, okay?"
Thomas, nine, walked taller after those visits. At home he was the youngest of four and hardly noticed.
Then Farida Aunty from next door saw him leave the back room and asked where he had been. Thomas shrugged. "It's a secret."
Farida Aunty knelt to his eye level. "Thank you for telling me that much. Grown-ups shouldn't ask children for secrets. You're not in any trouble." She walked him home, sat with his Amma, and together they called the school counsellor that evening.

qa.q: Where was the shop Thomas stopped at?
qa.a: The shop was by the paddy fields.

qa.q: Why did Thomas walk taller after the visits?
qa.a: He felt proud and special, which mattered because at home, as the youngest of four, he was hardly noticed.

qa.q: What did Farida Aunty do right when Thomas said "It's a secret"?
qa.a: She stayed calm, knelt to his eye level, told him he was not in trouble, walked him home and called the school counsellor with his Amma that evening.

qa.q: How might Thomas's Amma feel when Farida Aunty explains?
qa.a: She may feel worried and shaken, but grateful that Farida Aunty noticed and that they could act the same evening.

grounding: A boy given treats, games and praise by a shopkeeper who asks for secrecy feels special, and a neighbour notices and acts the same day.

passage:
I'm Harsha. When I was nine, my tuition sir started giving me chocolates. Only me. He said I was the cleverest one. He gave me extra marks on tests and a small toy car.
He said, "This is our secret. The others will be jealous." I felt special.
Then he said I should stay back after tuition, alone, for "special lessons," and not tell Mummy because she'd stop the classes. My stomach felt funny. I liked him. I didn't know why I felt scared.
That evening I told my big sister Rekha. She stopped what she was doing and listened. Then she held my hand and took me straight to Mummy.
Mummy didn't shout. She said, "Thank you for telling me. You did nothing wrong." She called the tuition centre owner and the police helpline that same night. I never went back.

qa.q: What did the tuition sir give Harsha?
qa.a: Chocolates, extra marks on tests and a small toy car.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when told to stay back alone and not tell Mummy?
qa.a: Harsha felt confused and scared, liking the tutor but sensing something was wrong, with a funny feeling in the stomach.

qa.q: What did Rekha and Mummy do that was right?
qa.a: Rekha listened and took Harsha straight to Mummy, who thanked Harsha, said it wasn't Harsha's fault, and called the centre owner and police helpline that night.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt when Harsha told her?
qa.a: Rekha probably felt worried and protective, which is why she stopped everything and took Harsha to Mummy at once.

grounding: A child recalls feeling special from a tutor's gifts and secret treatment, becoming confused when asked to hide things, and adults acting the same day.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Thursday. Written by Rukmini.
Rajni, Class 4, came to my room at lunch to show me a new pencil box. She said a neighbour uncle gives her gifts every week: pencils, a bracelet, chocolates. He lets her play games on his phone in his flat, "our special time." He told her not to tell her parents, because "they'll think you're greedy."
She was smiling and proud. She clearly feels important. She doesn't think anything is wrong.
I stayed calm. I told her, "Thank you for telling me, Rajni. You haven't done anything wrong. No grown-up should ask you to keep secrets from your parents."
I informed our safeguarding lead immediately. We called Rajni's mother to school this afternoon and explained gently. She is keeping Rajni away from the neighbour and has contacted the child helpline with our support. I will see Rajni again tomorrow.

qa.q: What did the neighbour uncle give Rajni?
qa.a: Pencils, a bracelet, chocolates.

qa.q: How does Rajni feel about the neighbour uncle's gifts?
qa.a: Rajni feels proud and special, and doesn't sense anything is wrong.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do the same day?
qa.a: The counsellor thanked Rajni, told her she wasn't to blame, informed the safeguarding lead, and called her mother to school that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Rajni's mother feel hearing this?
qa.a: Her mother would likely feel shocked and frightened, and also grateful the counsellor noticed and acted.

grounding: A counsellor notes a child made to feel special by an adult's gifts and secret games, not knowing it is wrong, and acts to protect her that day.

passage:
Tuesday
Coach Sir says I'm his favourite in the whole swimming club. He gives me the good lane and juice from his bag, only me. He says, "Don't tell the others, Jasleen." I feel so special!
But today he said I should stay after practice when everyone goes, and not tell Mumma because she'll worry for nothing.
My tummy felt weird. I like Coach Sir. So why can't Mumma know?
When Manjula Masi picked me up, I told her. She stopped the scooter and listened to all of it. "Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing, and you're not in trouble."
Masi called Mumma right away. Tonight they went to the club office together to tell the manager. I'll practise in the other batch now.

qa.q: What did Coach Sir give Jasleen after practice?
qa.a: Juice from his bag, only for Jasleen.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when told to stay back and not tell Mumma?
qa.a: Jasleen felt confused and uneasy, with a weird tummy feeling, because she liked the coach but didn't understand why Mumma couldn't know.

qa.q: What did Manjula Masi do that was right?
qa.a: She stopped to listen fully, thanked Jasleen, said Jasleen wasn't in trouble, called Mumma at once, and went with Mumma to the club office that night.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel when Masi called?
qa.a: Mumma would likely feel frightened and protective, and relieved that Jasleen told Masi.

grounding: A child's diary shows feeling special from a coach's favouritism and secrets, confusion when asked to hide things, and adults acting the same day.

passage: At the recharge shop in the village, Amandeep-uncle always had a toffee ready for Naveen. Lately he let Naveen play games on his phone in the back room, and gave him a shiny cricket cap. "You're my favourite," he said. "Our special game is a secret, okay?" Naveen felt proud and grown-up, but his tummy felt odd as he walked home. That evening Dadi saw the cap. "Who gave this, beta?" Naveen looked at his feet. "It's a secret." Dadi put down the rolling pin and sat beside him. "You did right to tell me. Grown-ups shouldn't ask children for secrets from family. You're not in trouble." Before dinner she had called Naveen's father home and phoned the head of the village child protection committee.

qa.q: What did Amandeep-uncle give Naveen?
qa.a: A toffee and a shiny cricket cap, and he let Naveen play games on his phone.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the special attention?
qa.a: Naveen felt proud and grown-up, yet his tummy felt odd on the way home, a sign he was confused.

qa.q: How did Dadi respond, and why was it right?
qa.a: She stayed calm, said Naveen did right and was not in trouble, and called his father and the child protection committee the same evening, protecting him without scaring him.

qa.q: How might Dadi have felt when Naveen said the cap was a secret?
qa.a: Dadi likely felt alarmed and protective, but she kept her worry quiet, stayed calm with Naveen and acted before dinner.

grounding: Shows a child given gifts, phone games and a secret by an adult, feeling important but uneasy, and a grandmother who responds calmly the same day.
